question: Tell me about Yakov Kesselbrener: Between Heroism and Destruction
markdown:
## Testimony and meaning

The memorial book’s Hebrew/Yiddish entry, [Yakov Kesselbrener: Between Heroism and Destruction (Testimony)](/communities/lukow/records/testimony_yaakov), appears in *Sefer Lukow* under the title “Between Valor and Annihilation,” listed among the book’s Holocaust-era accounts. The supplied evidence identifies Yakov—also recorded as [Jacob Kesselbrener](/communities/lukow/records/mention_bf0880221be2838779ce23d7)—as the narrator or subject of a testimony concerning the final liquidation of Łuków’s ghetto, escape, hiding, armed resistance, and the murder of his family. Because the English heading and summary are editorial layers and the OCR is uncertain, these details should ultimately be checked against scan 474, printed page 470, and the original text “יעקב קעסעלברענער.” *Sefer Lukow* was published in Tel Aviv in 1968 as a memorial to the destroyed community. ([JewishGen, *The Book of Lukow*](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/lukow.html))

The testimony’s central tragedy is recorded separately as the [Murder of the Kesselbrener family](/communities/lukow/records/event_candidate_2882cdecba1b0f6a221363e3): the [Kesselbrener family](/communities/lukow/records/mention_cadccf2ba27b8bdf88169d74) was hidden in a Polish person’s home in Domina and was later discovered and murdered. The evidence does not identify the hiding family’s individual members or establish precisely how Yakov escaped. It does, however, preserve the contrast implied by the title: survival through flight and resistance coexisted with the destruction of those closest to him. [Eliezer Kesselbrenner](/communities/lukow/records/mention_caa877184ad96495149ca610) is mentioned in connection with an attempted crossing involving the Bermans, but the supplied records do not prove his relationship to Yakov.

## Łuków in context

This account belongs to the final phase of the Łuków ghetto’s destruction. German authorities surrounded the ghetto in September 1942; the first major liquidation began on October 5, with deportations to Treblinka and mass shootings in the town. Further deportations and killings followed in October and December, and the last prisoners were deported on May 2, 1943. ([Virtual Shtetl, “Getto w Łukowie”](https://sztetl.org.pl/en/towns/l/729-lukow/116-sites-of-martyrdom/48334-getto-w-lukowie)) Łuków had previously been a major Jewish center, with organized religious, educational, cultural, labor, and Zionist institutions; its prewar Jewish population formed roughly half the town’s inhabitants, and only about 150 Łuków Jews survived the Holocaust. ([History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w); [Virtual Shtetl, community history](https://sztetl.org.pl/pl/miejscowosci/l/729-lukow/99-historia-spolecznosci/137635-historia-spolecznosci))

The surname itself appears in wider regional Jewish records, including a Ryki memorial necrology listing Kesselbrener Szymon, Samuel, Choncze, and a Kesselbrenner family headed by Chaim, including Jakob. This demonstrates the name’s regional presence but does **not** establish a documented connection to Yakov of Łuków. ([Ryki memorial necrology](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/ryki/ryk585.html))
